title: Face with Thermometer Emoji 🤒 Meaning: “I'm Sick”
description: The face with thermometer emoji 🤒 says you have a fever, the flu or just feel awful. See when to send it, what it means from others and how it differs from 😷.
summary: The 🤒 face with thermometer means the sender is sick, usually with a fever, cold or flu. It is the clearest emoji for calling in ill, canceling plans or asking for sympathy. Occasionally it is used figuratively for being lovesick or for something so impressive it is described as sick.
meaning: A thermometer held in the mouth is a childhood image of being kept home from school, and that is the mood 🤒 carries. It says I have a temperature, I am in bed, do not expect much from me. Unlike the mask emoji, it leaves no doubt about whether the sender is ill or just being careful.

The emoji is used for almost any ordinary illness: flu, a stomach bug, a bad cold, the day after a vaccine, even a rough hangover when the sender wants sympathy. The worried brows and tight mouth make it look sorry for itself, which is part of the point. It invites a get well soon, an offer of soup or permission to rest.

People also send it about others. Parents use it to report a child home from daycare, pet owners for a trip to the vet, and friends attach it to a message asking how a sick person is doing. In that direction it expresses concern rather than a request for it, and it often comes with a heart.

Figurative uses exist but are minor. Some people play on the slang sense of sick, meaning excellent, and add 🤒 to praise a song or a trick. Others use it for a fever of a different kind, such as being lovesick or obsessed with a new show. These read as jokes and rely on the surrounding words.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: This is its home. A message like can't make it 🤒 needs no further explanation, and most people answer with sympathy rather than questions. Sending it by itself to a partner or parent is a small request to be looked after.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: It is common in sick-day messages to a team and as a status that explains why you are offline. It keeps the tone light while still being clear. For a formal notice to HR or a client, plain words are better, with the emoji left for the team chat.

contexts.label: For parents and families
contexts.body: School and family group chats are full of it during winter. It reports who has caught what, warns other parents about a bug going around the classroom and explains a last-minute absence from a birthday party or a carpool without a long apology.

contexts.label: On social media
contexts.body: It captions photos of blankets, tea and tissues, and sits in posts asking for remedy or show recommendations while stuck in bed. In music and sports comments, a 🤒 may instead mean the performance was sick in the complimentary sense.

examples.meaning: The sender has a real fever and is resting.

examples.text: Can someone cover my shift tomorrow? 🤒
examples.meaning: They are too ill to work and need a replacement.

examples.text: Poor Mia is home again 🤒 third bug this month
examples.meaning: A parent reporting that their child is sick.
A check-in on someone who has been unwell.
Slang praise: the solo was sick, meaning extremely good.

examples.text: Got my flu shot yesterday and now 🤒
examples.meaning: Feeling run down as a side effect of a vaccine.

combos.meaning: Sick in bed and not going anywhere today.
A full cold or flu, with both a temperature and constant sneezing.
Resting and treating an illness with tea, soup or other home comforts.
Unwell and on medication, or about to take some.

confusedWith.difference: 😷 may mean illness, caution, a clinic visit or a bad smell. 🤒 is narrower and more certain: the person has symptoms, most likely a fever, right now.
🤕 is for injuries and pain, such as a bump, a headache or a hard knock. 🤒 is for infections and feeling ill. One is hurt, the other is sick.
🥵 is red, sweating and panting from heat, exertion or attraction. It is sometimes used for a fever, but 🤒 is the conventional choice when you mean an actual illness.

avoid: Do not use it to fake an illness to someone who may later find out you were fine.
Avoid it for serious or chronic conditions unless the person affected uses it that way themselves, because it suggests a short, minor bug.
Skip the slang sense of sick with people who might think you are actually unwell.
design: A yellow face with furrowed, sloping eyebrows, a frown and a thermometer sticking out of one side of the mouth. Most vendors draw an old-style glass thermometer with a red line, and a few show a digital one. Some add flushed red cheeks or a slightly pale face. The expression is consistently miserable across platforms.

faqs.q: What does 🤒 mean in a text?
faqs.a: Nearly always that the sender is ill. If it comes with a canceled plan, that is the reason. If it follows a question about you, the person is asking whether you are still feeling unwell. Slang uses are rare and usually obvious from context.

The thermometer face is for sickness such as flu and fevers. The head bandage face is for physical injury, headaches and feeling battered. If you fell off a bike use 🤕; if you caught what your coworker had, use 🤒.

Sometimes. Because sick is slang for impressive, a few people add 🤒 to compliments, often with a fire emoji. It is a niche use, more common in music, skating and gaming communities, and it can confuse anyone who takes it literally.

faqs.q: Is it okay to use 🤒 when calling in sick to work?
faqs.a: In an informal team chat, yes, and it is widely understood. In an email to a manager you do not know well, or any message that forms part of an official record, write it out plainly and leave the emoji off.
